analysis.title: Tin hats and tunnel vision: Equities and higher yields
key_insights: The US 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.5% at the end of June to around 5.3% at the end of September 2026. The report says this is elevated but not unprecedented: yields approached this level in 2023 and regularly exceeded it before the 2008-2009 financial crisis.

Equities can keep advancing through periods of rising yields as long as earnings stay supportive. Over the past 30 years, sector and industry-group returns have been closely linked to changes in earnings expectations in both rising and falling yield regimes.

Inflation, tighter monetary policy and higher term premia have pushed bond yields structurally higher since the 1997-2020 period of rising profits and falling yields. Equities have still advanced, supported by strong earnings and AI-related investment.

World earnings expectations grew 29.5% year-over-year in September, and estimates rose 8% during the third quarter. All 11 sectors in the MSCI World Index recorded year-over-year growth in earnings expectations.
Semiconductors and semiconductor equipment are a clear outlier, with exceptional increases in both earnings expectations and share prices. Earnings have also been resilient outside this group.
The near-term risk is that current strong fundamentals are extrapolated too far into the future, not that returns are disconnected from fundamentals.

The margin for error has narrowed. Higher yields raise the return available outside equities, and the market depends heavily on the AI investment cycle (data centres, semiconductors, related infrastructure). A slowdown in AI investment or profitability could challenge expectations.
Investors face two distinct risks: earnings expectations may disappoint, or valuations may compress as higher discount rates compete for capital.

The authors argue for diversification, valuation discipline and attention to balance-sheet quality rather than abandoning equities. They say defensive equity allocations and disciplined risk control may prove valuable again, and that the 'tin hat' may not yet be necessary but should be kept close.

sector_views.rationale: Described as a clear outlier on both earnings expectation increases and share price gains. The report flags stretched extremes but gives no explicit rating.

earnings_insights: World earnings expectations (MSCI World, a forward-looking consensus measure, not a reported print) grew 29.5% year-over-year in September 2026.
Earnings estimates for the MSCI World rose 8% during Q3 2026. All 11 sectors showed year-over-year growth in earnings expectations.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Up from 4.5% at the end of June. Higher yields increase the return available outside equities and raise the risk of valuation compression.
Starting point for the third-quarter bond sell-off.

risk_factors: Earnings expectations disappoint after being extrapolated too far.
Valuation compression as higher discount rates intensify competition for capital.
A slowdown in AI investment or profitability.
Renewed inflation pressures and heightened geopolitical tensions.
vol_and_positioning: The report describes the equity market as having concentrated leadership and an unusual dependence on the AI investment cycle, which leaves more room for disappointment.
geopolitical: The report cites heightened geopolitical tensions as part of the backdrop, without naming specific events or actors.

tension_points.bull_case: Equities can keep advancing through rising yields if earnings stay supportive. World earnings expectations grew 29.5% year-over-year in September and all 11 sectors showed growth, backed by AI investment.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher yields raise the return available outside equities. Earnings expectations may disappoint, or valuations may compress as higher discount rates compete for capital, with the market unusually dependent on AI investment.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in AI investment or profitability, or earnings expectations that disappoint.
